Simple. They'd form a small team to manage a custom distro based on, say, Debian, create a local copy of the upstream repositories, create tools to manage updates to those repositories and processes to install the OS from the internal repositories on new systems. That way the in-house team could control when their repositories are upgraded from the upstream and pass through only those updates they deemed appropriate.

I did this for a company I worked for, except that the targets were not employee systems but proprietary embedded systems that we based on Linux and sold to the general public. I built a system & web app that allowed customer systems to securely phone home using public key crypto to check for updates. Logs and package data were exported to the server following every update. And we could even install custom one-off / serial-number-specific packages on particular systems if necessary. A postgres database tracked every package installed on every customer system, and thus we could tell at a glance who had upgraded and who hadn't, what software was in use and what software we could officially retire.

A neat system that worked well for several years until I got fed up with the company's management and left. While walking out the door I asked if I could release portions of the system open source knowing full well I'd be refused. And sure enough, I was.

The point to take home is that I was one person and did the whole thing inside of a year. That's a trivial cost. And M$ better watch out -- the more they try to ass fuck businesses, the more likely businesses are to consider bringing OS management in house.
